messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald is a 58-year-old dentist of Canadian descent, currently living with his long-term partner in a mid-sized American city. He was referred for psychological assessment following a significant decline in his professional functioning and a near-complete withdrawal from social life. His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in the severe range, and what emerges across the intake and early sessions is a man whose world has contracted almost beyond recognition since an encounter with police approximately fourteen months ago.

Gerald had been driving home from an evening continuing education seminar when he was pulled over in an unfamiliar neighbourhood. What began as a routine stop escalated within seconds: he was ordered out of the vehicle at gunpoint, forced face-down onto the asphalt, and held there — a knee pressed into the centre of his back — for what he estimates was close to eight minutes. He remembers the sound of radio static and shouted commands, and the specific sensation of gravel cutting into his cheek. No charges were ever filed. No apology was offered. The officers involved were not disciplined. Gerald drove himself home that night and told no one for three weeks.

The memory of the event has a quality he struggles to articulate — he describes it as feeling like it happened to someone else, a kind of footage from another person's life that nonetheless arrives with full sensory force. When it surfaces, he hears the radio static again, and he feels the pressure and pain across his upper back and ribs as though the weight has never fully lifted. These intrusive returns are not neutral. Each time the memory floods back, Gerald finds himself arriving at the same dark conclusion: that there must be something about him — some quality others can read — that invited what happened. He cannot fully articulate what that quality is, but the certainty that it exists has settled into him like a belief he never consciously chose. The memory does not simply replay; it prosecutes him. And because the prosecution never ends, he has come to feel that his life as he knew it has been destroyed — that the person who drove to that seminar no longer exists, and that nothing adequate has been done to account for what was taken from him.

The sense of injustice and self-blame that the memory generates feeds back into how he holds the memory itself: he ruminates on it, turns it over, searching for the moment he could have prevented it, and in doing so keeps the event perpetually present and unresolved. When the memory arrives, it also arrives as threat — the world it conjures is one in which danger comes without warning, from figures of authority, from strangers, from any situation he cannot fully control. He now feels threatened by strangers approaching him in ordinary situations, including, with increasing frequency, patients entering his operatory. He has begun positioning himself in his dental chair so that he always has a clear sightline to the door, and he scans the waiting room when he passes through it in a way his receptionist has quietly noticed.

The threat he carries with him has reshaped his behaviour across months. He avoids anything he anticipates might be stressful — he has declined two professional conferences, stopped attending his partner's family gatherings, and reduced his patient load by nearly a third. More broadly, he avoids any emotional activation at all, positive or negative, as though feeling anything risks opening a door he cannot close. He no longer watches films, avoids music he once loved, and has described meals with his partner as something he endures rather than enjoys. This emotional blunting has not protected him; instead, the avoidance has kept him from processing what happened, and the memory remains as raw as it was in the early weeks. The strategies that were meant to contain his distress have quietly confirmed his belief that he is permanently damaged — that a man who must manage his life so carefully must have something fundamentally wrong with him.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was his partner's direct statement that she no longer recognised him. He arrives at sessions sitting with his back to the wall, watching the door. What he most fears is that the clinician will confirm what he already suspects. What he most hopes — though he says it with little conviction — is that he is wrong.
